common_name: Southern Gentleman Winterberry Holly (Male Pollinator for Late-Blooming Winterberry Cultivars)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; as a male clone Southern Gentleman never fruits itself but must be sited within about 50 feet of late-blooming female winterberries to set them in berry.

directions: Southern Gentleman is a dense, upright male winterberry selected specifically as a late-season pollinizer for southern-blooming female cultivars such as Winter Red, Winter Gold, and Sparkleberry, whose flowers open too late for earlier males like Jim Dandy to service. One plant can pollinate roughly six to ten females if kept within pollinating range, so it is usually tucked into the back of a hedgerow or wildlife thicket rather than featured as a specimen. Though it carries no berries of its own, its small spring flowers are worked heavily by native bees, and its dense multi-stemmed thickets provide valuable nesting cover for songbirds. Plant in consistently moist, acidic soil and avoid limy or dry sites, which winterberry tolerates poorly regardless of sex.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Connecticut Home & Garden Education Center

common_name: Afterglow Winterberry Holly (Compact Orange-Red Berried Female Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant female container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, siting an early-flowering male such as Jim Dandy or Southern Gentleman nearby for pollination and fruit set.

directions: Introduced by an Indiana nursery in the 1970s, Afterglow is a notably compact winterberry selection, staying under six feet, that still produces an unusually heavy set of soft orange-red berries rather than the typical fire-engine red of most cultivars. The berries hold their color and cling to the bare branches through much of the winter, making this a dependable food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other overwintering birds once other soft fruits have been stripped from the landscape. Its smaller mature size fits foundation plantings, rain gardens, and pond edges where full-size winterberries would crowd the space. Give it consistently moist, acidic soil, since prolonged dryness quickly stresses this wetland-edge native.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Connecticut Home & Garden Education Center

common_name: Edith Wilder Sweetshrub (Extra-Fragrant Mahogany-Red Flowered Carolina Allspice)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Edith Wilder was selected specifically for unusually strong, consistent fragrance in a species whose scent otherwise varies widely between seedlings.

directions: Traced to a clone collected around 1919 at what became the Scott Arboretum in Pennsylvania, Edith Wilder produces unusually large, two-inch mahogany-red flowers with a strong, fruity perfume that ranks among the most reliably fragrant of any named sweetshrub selection. The glossy dark foliage turns clear yellow in autumn on a dense, upright-spreading shrub well suited to a woodland edge or shaded native border. Like the species, its strap-petaled spring flowers are pollinated primarily by sap and carrion beetles drawn to the fruity scent, an unusual pollination strategy that supports beneficial insects most spring-flowering shrubs ignore. Because fragrance intensity is the whole point of this selection, source rooted cuttings from a reputable propagator rather than seedlings, which will not come true.

common_name: Purpureus Sweetshrub (Historic Copper-Red New-Growth Carolina Allspice)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; foliage color is most pronounced with some direct sun and turns a plainer olive-green in denser shade.

directions: Formally described nearly a century ago, Purpureus is the historic source clone behind most of today's dark-leaved sweetshrub cultivars, distinguished by coppery-red new growth, most pronounced on the leaf undersides, that ages toward green as summer progresses. Its dark maroon, strap-petaled flowers carry the same fruity fragrance as the species and open in late spring, drawing the sap beetles and flies that serve as Calycanthus's primary pollinators. Once nearly lost to cultivation, it survives mainly in arboretum collections and specialty nurseries today, making it a worthwhile find for anyone assembling a historically significant native shade border. Grow it as an understory large shrub with light dappled shade for the healthiest habit, and expect the same easy, low-maintenance care as straight-species sweetshrub.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

common_name: Burgundy Spice Sweetshrub (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Native Allspice)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Burgundy Spice was bred from the historic purpureus form and holds its dark color better through summer heat than most other purple-leaved sweetshrubs.

directions: A modern New Jersey-bred selection out of the old purpureus lineage, Burgundy Spice carries glossy, near-black purple foliage from spring through the hottest part of summer before shifting to yellow and orange in fall, a striking foliage effect layered on top of the species' usual charms. Its maroon, mango-and-pineapple-scented flowers open in late spring and are visited by the sap beetles and flies that pollinate sweetshrub, an easy nectar stop for these overlooked pollinators in a partly shaded native border. Left alone it slowly suckers into a broad multi-stemmed colony, useful for naturalizing a shaded slope or woodland edge, or can be kept tidier with occasional removal of root suckers. Prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's new growth.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Harvest Moon Witch Hazel (Late Fall-Blooming Lemon-Yellow Native Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Harvest Moon flowers noticeably later than typical common witch hazel, often waiting until the surrounding leaves have dropped.

directions: Selected by a Connecticut plantsman, Harvest Moon delays its bloom until very late fall, frequently opening around the full moon after Thanksgiving once its own leaves and those of the surrounding canopy have already dropped, which lets its slightly larger, strap-petaled lemon-yellow flowers show up clearly against bare branches rather than being hidden by foliage. That unusually late bloom window makes it one of the last nectar sources of the year for any flies, gnats, and cold-hardy moths still active before winter fully sets in. Its loosely vase-shaped, multi-stemmed habit tolerates considerably more shade than most flowering shrubs, making it a good choice for a woodland understory planting rather than an open border. Prune only lightly if needed right after flowering to maintain shape, since it requires little routine maintenance once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Mohonk Red Witch Hazel (Brick-Red Fall-Blooming Native Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Mohonk Red tolerates deeper shade than most flowering native shrubs and was originally found growing wild in a New York nature preserve.

directions: Discovered growing wild at a nature preserve in New York's Shawangunk Mountains and later introduced through a major botanical institution, Mohonk Red is an unusually floriferous common witch hazel selection whose spidery, strap-shaped petals are red at the base and fade to pale yellow at the tips, giving the whole plant a warm brick-red glow in October and November against a backdrop of matching gold fall foliage. Blooming this late in the season, after most insects have gone dormant, it still draws the cold-tolerant owlet moths and other winter-active pollinators that keep working on mild fall days, an easy way to extend pollinator value deep into the off-season. As one of the more shade-tolerant flowering native shrubs available, it thrives as a large-scale understory planting beneath deciduous trees where little else blooms. It needs only minimal pruning and tolerates a wide range of soils as long as drainage is reasonable.
